lead: Cloud programming means breaking work into units that run across many machines, then choosing a platform that supplies those machines, storage and messaging. This unit moves from parallel and task models through MapReduce and Spark to AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and open-source IaaS, ending with CloudSim. After it, a student can read a workload, pick a programming model, map it to provider services, and estimate or simulate a schedule.
about: The unit connects programming models to real cloud platforms. 5.1 sets the vocabulary for parallel and distributed work: threads, message passing and data parallelism. 5.2 adds high-throughput task models, and 5.3 reduces data-intensive work to map, shuffle and reduce. 5.4 shows how Spark keeps data in memory for iterative and streaming jobs. 5.5, 5.6 and 5.7 compare the three big public clouds — AWS, Google Cloud and Azure — through compute, storage, networking and monitoring. 5.8 opens the private-cloud stack with Eucalyptus, OpenStack and OpenNebula. 5.9 closes with CloudSim, where schedules such as SJF can be tested without buying hardware. Each chapter builds on the one before: model, then framework, then provider, then simulator.

chapters.idea: A cloud program must choose a parallel model — shared-memory threads, message passing or data parallelism — that matches how its work communicates and fails.
chapters.depth: Cover fundamental aspects: decomposition, granularity, communication, synchronization, load balance, latency and partial failure. Compare shared-memory threads, message-passing processes, data-parallel workers and master-worker. Include concurrent computing, thread programming, multithreading with Aneka, and Aneka Threads as a cloud thread model. Some syllabi call this cloud application programming. Keep formulas simple: speedup and Amdahl's law.
chapters.figure: blocks: four worker threads or processes feed one cloud application, with a model-choice box for shared memory, message passing and data parallel; aria: three programming models feed a single cloud application.
chapters.example: A program adds 8,000,000 numbers. Four worker threads each add 2,000,000 numbers. Sequential time is 160 ms. Thread creation costs 5 ms in total and the final merge costs 5 ms. Find the ideal speedup and the actual speedup. Answer: each thread does 40 ms of work in parallel. Actual time = 40 ms + 5 ms + 5 ms = 50 ms. Ideal speedup = 160 ÷ 40 = 4×. Actual speedup = 160 ÷ 50 = 3.2×.
chapters.trap: Threads share one address space and do not by themselves spread across VMs. Concurrency is not automatically parallelism; speedup is bounded by the serial part and coordination cost.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 parallel versus distributed computing; Unit 2 web services and REST.
chapters.leave: OS thread scheduling and language APIs; virtualization to Unit 3; security to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: High-throughput computing keeps many independent tasks flowing through a pool of workers, optimizing completed work per hour rather than one job's latency.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in depth; keep it shorter. Cover HTC versus HPC, task-based application models, bag-of-tasks, task dependencies as a DAG, master-worker scheduling, and Aneka Task-Based Programming. Include the Aneka task model and developing applications with it. Mention throughput, makespan and scheduling overhead.
chapters.figure: gantt: 12 worker lanes run 600 independent 4 min tasks over 200 min ideal, with a 0.5 min task overhead widening it to 225 min; aria: many short task bars fill twelve worker lanes on a timeline.
chapters.example: 600 independent tasks, each 4 min, run on 12 workers. Scheduling overhead is 0.5 min per task and is paid on the worker. Ideal makespan = 600 × 4 ÷ 12 = 200 min. Actual makespan = 600 × (4 + 0.5) ÷ 12 = 225 min. Throughput = 600 ÷ 225 = 2.67 tasks/min.
chapters.trap: HTC maximizes completed tasks, not one task's latency. Tasks must be independent or obey a DAG; adding workers can hurt when scheduling overhead dominates.
chapters.leave: MapReduce to Chapter 5.3; detailed Aneka installation to a lab.

chapters.idea: MapReduce expresses data-intensive work as map functions that emit key-value pairs, a shuffle that groups by key, and reduce functions that combine each group.
chapters.depth: Cover map and reduce signatures, input splits, shuffle/sort, combiner, partitioner, fault tolerance by re-execution, and word count. Use information retrieval and page ranking as MapReduce examples. Name Hadoop MapReduce as an implementation. Keep HDFS and GFS details out; Unit 4 owns them.
chapters.figure: blocks: input splits → map → shuffle/sort → reduce → output for word count; aria: a pipeline groups map output by key before reduce.
chapters.example: Input lines: cat dog cat / dog / cat. Give map output, per-line combiner output, shuffled groups and reduce output. Map: (cat,1),(dog,1),(cat,1); (dog,1); (cat,1). Per-line combiner: cat→2, dog→1; dog→1; cat→1. Shuffle with combiners: cat→[2,1], dog→[1,1]. Reduce: cat→3, dog→2.
chapters.trap: Shuffle sends all values for one key to one reducer, so one hot key can dominate. Combiners are optional and must be associative and commutative; map output is not final output.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1; Unit 4 distributed file systems for HDFS and GFS context.
chapters.leave: HDFS/GFS and BigTable internals to Unit 4; Spark to Chapter 5.4.

chapters.idea: Spark keeps immutable distributed data in memory and rebuilds lost parts from lineage, which suits iterative and streaming jobs better than repeated disk-based MapReduce.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in depth; keep it shorter. Cover RDDs, transformations, actions, lazy evaluation, lineage, cache and persist, and DataFrames. Include Spark Streaming micro-batches and graph frameworks such as GraphLab and GraphX. Compare with MapReduce.
chapters.figure: graph: RDD lineage DAG from textFile → flatMap → map → reduceByKey → collect, with a cached RDD marked; aria: a directed acyclic graph of lazy transformations ending in an action.
chapters.example: Input lines: a b a / b c. Run lines.flatMap(split).map(word → (word,1)).reduceByKey(add).collect(). FlatMap gives a,b,a,b,c. Map gives (a,1),(b,1),(a,1),(b,1),(c,1). Reduce gives (a,2),(b,2),(c,1).
chapters.trap: Transformations are lazy; no job runs until an action. collect() pulls all results to the driver, caching uses memory, and long lineage slows recovery.
chapters.leave: Cluster tuning and provider setup to Chapters 5.5–5.7; detailed graph algorithms to a graph course.

chapters.idea: AWS supplies modular cloud building blocks: EC2 for compute, EBS and S3 for storage, VPC and security groups for networking, and SQS or SNS for communication.
chapters.depth: Cover EC2 instances and AMIs, instance types, EBS block storage versus S3 object storage, VPC subnets, route tables, security groups, load balancing, SQS/SNS, CloudWatch monitoring and automation. Include basic VM creation and web-app hosting workflow. Compare providers only at overview level. Do not quote prices; say prices change by region and time.
chapters.figure: blocks: VPC 10.0.0.0/16 with public subnet 10.0.1.0/24 holding 2 web EC2 instances, private subnet 10.0.2.0/24 holding 1 DB EC2 instance, plus S3 and SQS; aria: three compute instances split across two subnets with storage and a queue.
chapters.example: A web app needs 2 web servers, 1 database, 100 GB image store and a job queue. Use VPC 10.0.0.0/16, public subnet 10.0.1.0/24, private subnet 10.0.2.0/24. Place 2 web EC2 instances, 1 DB EC2 instance, one S3 bucket and one SQS queue. Open port 443 from the internet to the web security group and port 3306 from the web security group to the DB security group. State which resources sit in each subnet and which flows are allowed.
chapters.trap: A security group is a stateful instance firewall, not a subnet. S3 is object storage, not a mountable block disk. A public subnet needs a route to an internet gateway.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 service models; Unit 2 networking and load balancing.
chapters.leave: IAM detail to Unit 6; storage internals to Unit 4; VM internals to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Google App Engine is a managed PaaS that runs code with automatic scaling, while Google Cloud also offers IaaS and managed storage, messaging and monitoring.
chapters.depth: Cover App Engine standard and flexible environments, the project resource hierarchy, Compute Engine instances and images, VPC firewall rules, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, and Cloud Monitoring. Include a basic VM creation and web-app hosting path. Compare App Engine PaaS with AWS EC2 IaaS.
chapters.figure: blocks: client → App Engine front end → 1 automatic instance → Cloud Storage, with Pub/Sub as a side queue; aria: a managed request path with one auto-scaled instance.
chapters.example: An App Engine service receives 900 requests/min. Each request uses 30 ms CPU. Target CPU is 50%. One instance supplies 60 CPU-s/min at 100%. CPU needed = 900 × 0.03 s = 27 CPU-s/min. At 50% target, one instance supplies 30 CPU-s/min, so ceil(27 ÷ 30) = 1 instance. At 1,800 requests/min, need 54 CPU-s/min, so 2 instances.
chapters.trap: App Engine standard is a sandbox PaaS, not a raw VM. Scaling is automatic; capacity per instance must be computed at the target utilization, not at 100%.
chapters.leave: IAM detail to Unit 6; containers and Kubernetes to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Azure groups resources logically in resource groups, then connects VMs, storage and databases through virtual networks and network security rules.
chapters.depth: Cover subscriptions and resource groups, VMs and images, availability sets and zones, VNet and NSG rules, Blob/Files/Disk storage, Azure SQL Database, Azure Monitor and automation. Include a basic VM and web-app deployment path. Compare with AWS and Google Cloud.
chapters.figure: blocks: one Azure resource group with VNet 10.0.0.0/16, web subnet 10.0.1.0/24 with 2 web VMs, DB subnet 10.0.2.0/24 with Azure SQL Database, and a 100 GB Blob container; aria: two subnets inside a virtual network with compute, database and storage resources.
chapters.example: A resource group holds VNet 10.0.0.0/16, web subnet 10.0.1.0/24 with 2 web VMs, DB subnet 10.0.2.0/24 with Azure SQL Database, and a 100 GB Blob container. An NSG allows port 443 inbound from the internet to web and port 1433 from the web subnet to the DB subnet. List the resources and allowed flows.
chapters.trap: A resource group is a logical container, not a region. NSG rules are ordered allow/deny rules. Blob storage is not a file system; do not treat it as a disk.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 5.5 and 5.6 for comparison; Unit 3 VMs.
chapters.leave: IAM detail to Unit 6; hybrid networking to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Open-source IaaS platforms turn physical hosts and hypervisors into a private cloud with APIs, images, networks and storage services.
chapters.depth: Cover Eucalyptus architecture and EC2/S3 compatibility; OpenStack services Nova, Neutron, Cinder, Swift, Glance, Keystone and Horizon; OpenNebula front end and drivers; mention Apache CloudStack. Include installation overview and comparison. Do not turn it into a full install manual.
chapters.figure: stack: Horizon, Keystone, Nova, Neutron, Cinder, Swift, Glance; aria: an OpenStack service stack from dashboard and identity down to compute, network, block, object and image services.
chapters.example: A private cloud has 8 hosts, each 32 vCPU and 128 GB RAM. Reserve 1 host for the control plane. VMs need 4 vCPU and 8 GB RAM. At 1:1 CPU overcommit: usable vCPU = 7 × 32 = 224, so 224 ÷ 4 = 56 VMs; usable RAM = 7 × 128 = 896 GB, so 896 ÷ 8 = 112 VMs. The limit is 56 VMs. At 2:1 CPU overcommit, CPU allows 112 VMs, so the limit becomes 112 VMs.
chapters.trap: OpenStack is not a hypervisor; it manages hypervisors. The control plane needs reserved capacity. API compatibility with AWS does not mean every AWS service behaves identically.
chapters.leave: Production installation and troubleshooting to a lab; VM migration to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: CloudSim models data centres, hosts, VMs, brokers and cloudlets so scheduling policies such as SJF can be compared without real hardware.
chapters.depth: Cover CloudSim architecture: data centre, host, VM, broker, cloudlet, allocation policy and scheduler. Include running built-in examples, installing CloudSim, and analyzing output. Run SJF scheduling on one VM. Define MI (million instructions) and MIPS (million instructions per second). Keep real-provider deployment out.
chapters.figure: gantt: one 1000 MIPS VM runs SJF cloudlets in order 2000, 5000, 6000, 8000, 10000 MI, finishing at 2, 7, 13, 21, 31 s; aria: five bars in increasing length on one VM timeline.
chapters.example: One VM has 1000 MIPS. Five cloudlets have lengths 10000, 5000, 8000, 2000, 6000 MI. Run SJF on one VM. SJF order: 2000, 5000, 6000, 8000, 10000 MI. Times = 2, 5, 6, 8, 10 s. Completion times = 2, 7, 13, 21, 31 s. Waiting times = 0, 2, 7, 13, 21 s; average waiting = 43 ÷ 5 = 8.6 s. Average turnaround = 74 ÷ 5 = 14.8 s.
chapters.trap: Cloudlet length is in MI, not seconds; time = MI ÷ MIPS. SJF needs known lengths and can starve long jobs. CloudSim is a simulator, not a real cloud.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 scheduling; Chapter 5.8 optional for platform context.
chapters.leave: Real cloud deployment to Chapters 5.5–5.7; advanced scheduling policies to Unit 4.
